transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump is on his way back to Washington after a first-ever trilateral meeting with
the leaders of China and Russia.
NPR's Franco Ordonez reports the three focused on reducing nuclear arsenals but did not announce
any major breakthroughs.
The series of meetings, which also included one-on-one talks between the leaders, may
be remembered more though for the coziness Trump displayed with the longtime U.S. adversaries.
First with Putin.
Who is he?
He's my friend.
And then with Xi.
President Xi and I have formed an outstanding personal relationship.
It really is.
Some people are unhappy when they hear that, but I'm very happy about it.
The three leaders committed to a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks.
She called nuclear weapons a "sort of Damocles" hanging over humanity, according to Chinese
state media.
But they did not agree on what steps needed to be taken.
Franco Ordonez, NPR News.
Stock in the artificial intelligence company, Anthropic is now trading on the Nasdaq for
the first time.
NPR's Scott Horsley reports the move caps a record-breaking IPO.
Anthropic raised a whopping $81 billion with its first public stock sale, a move that
values the AI darling at a record $1.5 trillion.
Huge sums are being invested in the booming artificial intelligence business, although
some have begun to question whether those big bets will pay off.
Walmart is racking up bigger sales from bargain hunting customers, but the discount retailer
offered a cautious outlook for the holiday season.
Walmart sales grew nearly 3 percent in the most recent quarter.
And new applications for unemployment benefits inched higher last week, as 203,000 people
applied for jobless aid, applications are still low by historical standards, suggesting
that layoffs remain rare.
Scott Horsley, NPR News, Washington.
JPMorgan Chase says it believes it's third-party vendors were the targets of a cyberattack.
The major bank says some customers' names and email addresses may have been exposed.
The financial firm was among several major banks whose online banking services were disrupted
due to a bug this week.
State problems in recent days and weeks also affected the NSA, Apple, Microsoft Outlook,
and the FAA.
U.N. climate talks in Turkey are in their final days.
NPR's Rachel Waldos has an update.
Delegates from nearly 200 countries are in the last days of annual talks on how to cut
climate pollution and provide funding for developing countries.
Panama Environment Minister Juan Carlos Navarro told reporters the COP31 negotiations are not
moving fast enough to help countries like his.
Let's call a spade a spade.
The COPs have become an exercise in hypocrisy and futility.
Talks are set to end Friday, though they could drag into the weekend.
The U.S. is one of the few countries not participating.
Rachel Waldholz, NPR News, Antalya.
It's NPR.
The Mississippi Legislative Black Caucus and Democratic lawmakers are calling for an investigation
into Mississippi's voter roll system.
They argue the state's seen a spike of nearly 60,000 people listed as inactive on voter
rolls ahead of the midterm elections this month.
They say they want to make sure eligible voters were not blocked.
They point to the integration of data from a major credit reporting agency into the voter
roll maintenance process.
In the midterms, Democrats Scott Cullum defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith to become
the state's first black senator since Reconstruction.
Mississippi holds more statewide elections next year, including for governor.
Researchers are developing brain implants that can help restore people's speech and
movement.
NPR's Ping Wang has the latest.
A 58-year-old trained singer had lost much of her ability to speak and sing due to ALS,
a disease that destroys nerve cells that control muscle movement.
Maitreyi Wairakar is a neuroscientist at UC Davis.
She and her colleagues designed an implant that connects to parts of the singer's brain
related to speech, pitch and tone.
We designed a task to enable her to sing a musical scale.
We asked her to sing a typical major scale and we were able to decode all the notes that
she sang with very high accuracy.
The implant records her brain signals into a computer, which translates them into commands.
The technology is still largely experimental and was presented at the Society for Neuroscience
Conference. It's NPR News.

topics.text: Trump meets Putin and Xi in trilateral talks on reducing nuclear arsenals, no breakthroughs
Anthropic begins trading on Nasdaq after record $81 billion IPO valuing it at $1.5 trillion
Walmart reports stronger sales from bargain shoppers but cautious holiday outlook; jobless claims rise to 203,000
JPMorgan Chase says third-party vendors targeted in cyberattack; some customer emails may be exposed
UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey near end; Panama minister criticizes slow progress
Mississippi Black Caucus and Democrats seek investigation into spike in inactive voter roll listings
Researchers develop brain implant that decodes singing signals for ALS patient Maitreyi Wairakar's speech
